slides.notes:
RECAP: Session 11 : Cloud Provider Comparison
1. Major Cloud Providers: AWS, Azure & GCP as the primary players; IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud as additional enterprise cloud providers: market position & typical use cases
2. Service Equivalents Across Providers: Compute, storage, database & networking: same concept, different names (EC2/VM/Compute Engine; S3/Blob/Cloud Storage; RDS/Azure SQL/Cloud SQL for relational, DynamoDB/Cosmos DB/Firestore for NoSQL)
3. Machine Learning Service Comparison: Managed ML/AI offerings across AWS, Azure & GCP at a high level
4. Cloud Providers Walkthrough: The AWS console already familiar to students, shown alongside Azure Portal and GCP Console/Cloud Shell: the same task, back to back
5. Choosing a Provider: What genuinely differs (pricing, regions, service maturity, skills) vs what's cosmetic (naming, console layout)

Agenda for Today's Session
1. Security Goals: Confidentiality, integrity & availability in the cloud
2. Shared Responsibility Model: Security of the cloud vs security in the cloud
3. Responsibility by Service Model: Boundary shifts across IaaS, PaaS & SaaS
4. Common Misunderstandings: Provider vs customer duties; incidents caused by wrong assumptions
5. Defense in Depth: Layered controls: network, identity, data, application & monitoring

slides.title: Three Security Goals
slides.lead: Shared, multi-tenant hardware in the cloud raises the stakes for the same three goals: confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA)

points.text: Confidentiality: only authorised identities can read stored or moving data
Integrity: data and configuration stay unaltered without detection
Availability: workloads stay reachable despite hardware or zone failure

slides.notes: Build on the triad already known; frame it as a lock on a flat door, a tamper-proof meter, and a backup generator. Ask: why does sharing hardware with other tenants raise the stakes for all three goals?

slides.label: Analogy: housing society
slides.title: Three Security Goals
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A housing society gives each flat a locked door, a sealed power meter nobody can tamper with, and a backup generator that keeps the lift running: just as cloud systems lock access, detect tampering and keep running through failure.

Build on the triad already known; frame it as a lock on a flat door, a tamper-proof meter, and a backup generator. Ask: why does sharing hardware with other tenants raise the stakes for all three goals?

slides.title: Per Goal Controls
slides.lead: Providers offer managed services for each goal, but the customer must still enable and configure them

cells: Encryption at rest/in transit, access policies

cells.text: Key Management Service (KMS), S3 bucket policy
Multi-AZ RDS, Auto Scaling, ELB health checks

slides.notes: Point to each row and name the actual console screen: KMS key list, S3 versioning toggle, Auto Scaling group. Mention that encryption and versioning are configured once but checked continuously, which is a common interview question.

slides.title: Why It Matters
slides.lead: Because cloud resources are shared and reachable through internet-facing APIs, one misconfiguration or leaked credential can expose far more than a single owned server

points.text: Public storage bucket: one wrong setting exposes data to the internet
Noisy neighbour workload: can degrade availability if isolation is weak
Leaked credential: one key can reach many resources through APIs

slides.notes: Use the exposed bucket as the running example for the risk of pooled infrastructure. Who configures each of these controls differs by service, which the next idea addresses directly.

slides.title: Who Secures What
slides.lead: Cloud security never sits with one side alone. The Shared Responsibility Model (SRM) splits duties between provider and customer, so a breach often traces to a gap nobody actually owned

points.text: Security OF the cloud: provider secures physical infrastructure and virtualization
Security IN the cloud: customer secures data, access and configuration
The dividing line between the two shifts with the service model chosen

slides.notes: Explain SRM as a line dividing provider duties from customer duties, not a fixed task checklist. Mention that most reported breaches trace back to the customer's half, not provider infrastructure failure. Ask: can a learner name one example each of security 'of' and 'in' the cloud.

slides.label: Analogy: gated housing society
slides.title: Who Secures What
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A gated housing society's guard secures the main gate and compound walls; each resident still locks their own flat door and safe: exactly as the cloud provider secures the data centre while the customer secures what is configured inside their own account.

Explain SRM as a line dividing provider duties from customer duties, not a fixed task checklist. Mention that most reported breaches trace back to the customer's half, not provider infrastructure failure. Ask: can a learner name one example each of security 'of' and 'in' the cloud.

slides.title: Where Lines Are Drawn
slides.lead: The provider secures everything up to the virtualization layer, and the customer secures what they place on top. Managed services move this line upward. AWS documents the split on its Shared Responsibility Model page
slides.notes: Point to the table as the generic split, then name the AWS Shared Responsibility Model page as the actual reference checked per service. Note that a compliance certificate proves only the provider's side. A frequent interview question asks for one real misconfiguration caused by misreading this split.

slides.title: Where Lines Are Drawn

points.text: Split is checked per service, not applied as one blanket rule
Compliance certifications like ISO 27001 cover only the provider's side
Customer-side failures, such as open storage buckets, stay customer liability

slides.notes: Point to the table as the generic split, then name the AWS Shared Responsibility Model page as the actual reference checked per service. Note that a compliance certificate proves only the provider's side. A frequent interview question asks for one real misconfiguration caused by misreading this split.

slides.title: Impact Of Misapplication
slides.lead: Confusing provider duties with customer duties leaves protections unapplied, since the customer must configure and review every control on their half of the line. The split itself stays fixed; only its exact position moves across service models

points.text: Relaxing a default, such as opening a port or making a bucket public, is the customer's decision and risk
Provider SLAs cover infrastructure uptime, never customer configuration mistakes
Checking this split per service prevents the most common cloud breaches

props.caption: Customer-Side Gap, Not A Provider Failure

slides.notes: Summarise that the split's principle stays constant while its exact position moves by service model. Use a public storage bucket left open by a customer as the classic example. Ask: whose fault is a public bucket breach, the provider's or the account owner's.

slides.title: IaaS PaaS SaaS
slides.lead: The shared-responsibility line moves differently for each security duty (patching, network rules, encryption keys, access setup) as the stack moves from IaaS toward SaaS

points.text: OS patching is customer-owned only on IaaS
Network infrastructure shifts to the provider above IaaS, but access rules such as security groups stay with the customer
Encryption key choice stays with the customer through PaaS; provider-managed keys are the default
Access setup remains customer-owned across every service model

slides.notes: Explain that the earlier IaaS/PaaS/SaaS stack picture now gets a security lens, duty by duty. Ask: why does data access never cross to the provider's side?

slides.title: Customer Managed Layers
slides.lead: On IaaS, the customer runs a guest operating system on provider-managed hardware, so almost every security task above the hypervisor falls to the customer

points.text: Patches and hardens the guest OS and installed software
Configures security groups and network ACLs around the instance
Manages encryption keys for attached Elastic Block Store volumes
Sets access permissions for who can reach the instance

slides.notes: Point to security groups as the customer's main configuration duty on IaaS. Ask: who patches the EC2 operating system?

slides.title: Shared Mid Layer
slides.lead: Moving to PaaS, the provider takes over the runtime and OS patching that IaaS left with the customer, narrowing the customer's job to code and data

points.text: Provider patches the OS and runtime and applies engine updates in maintenance windows
Customer secures application code, access configuration and network access rules
Customer still controls data encryption settings and keys
Real-world location: Amazon RDS, a managed relational database service

slides.notes: Contrast this directly with the previous slide: the OS patching bullet that was customer-owned on IaaS is now provider-owned here. Mention RDS as the location an interviewer might probe for this exact boundary.

slides.title: Data And Access
slides.lead: At SaaS, the provider runs and secures the entire application stack, leaving the customer only the data placed inside it and who may access it

points.text: Provider secures infrastructure, application code and underlying platform fully
Customer classifies and protects the data stored inside the service
Customer configures user access, multi-factor login and sharing settings
Real-world location: Amazon Connect administration console, where security profiles set agent permissions

slides.notes: Stress that even on SaaS the customer is never fully off the hook: data and access configuration remain theirs. Point to the Amazon Connect console as where this duty is actually exercised.

slides.title: Who Secures What
slides.lead: Every security duty moves toward the provider as the stack rises, except one that never does: who controls data and who may access it
slides.notes: Use this table to summarise the whole boundary shift in one glance before moving to where teams get this boundary wrong. The data-and-access row is the one worth repeating in an interview answer.

slides.label: Quiz Time
slides.notes: Quiz on Security Goals, the Shared Responsibility Model and Responsibility by Service Model. Q1. Which security goal keeps data unaltered without detection? Answer: Integrity. Q2. Which AWS service supports confidentiality by managing encryption keys? Answer: Key Management Service (KMS). Q3. Who is responsible for security IN the cloud? Answer: The customer, for data, access and configuration. Q4. Up to which layer does the provider secure the stack? Answer: The hypervisor and virtualization layer. Q5. A customer leaves a storage bucket public. Does the provider's ISO 27001 certification or SLA cover it? Answer: No, it is a customer-side gap. Q6. On which service model does the customer patch the guest OS? Answer: Only on IaaS. Q7. On PaaS such as Amazon RDS, who patches the OS and runtime? Answer: The provider. Q8. Which duty stays with the customer on IaaS, PaaS and SaaS? Answer: Data and access control.

slides.title: Two Failure Directions
slides.lead: The shared responsibility line is clear on paper, but real incidents happen when either side assumes the other covers a task nobody actually performed

points.text: Customer assumes the provider covers it: believing AWS patches or secures customer data
Provider expects the customer to configure it: AWS documents bucket policies and security groups as customer tasks
Moving IaaS to PaaS to SaaS shifts the line, confusing which duty moved
Most breaches trace to a skipped step, not a platform flaw

slides.notes: Stress that the technology rarely fails; a missed assumption on either side does. Ask: which service model shift (IaaS to SaaS) most often causes this confusion, and why.

slides.title: Four Fault Lines
slides.lead: Certain duties get assumed away more often than others, because the provider's physical control of the hardware is mistaken for control of the setting itself

cells: Every RDS database is encrypted automatically
Customer enables encryption when creating the database
OS patches apply themselves on IaaS
No need to review IAM permissions

slides.notes: Walk through each row as a real scenario for an interview question. Point out that every 'Actual Duty' entry sits on the customer side of the responsibility line.

slides.title: Bucket Exposure Traced
slides.lead: A common breach pattern starts with one wrong assumption about a setting, then compounds silently until data is exposed

items: Developer creates an S3 bucket for application logs
Hits an access error and assumes loosening settings is harmless
S3 Block Public Access is switched off (it is on by default for new buckets)
Bucket policy grants read access to any user
Crawlers index the log files, exposing the data
Root cause: a skipped security-in-the-cloud step

slides.notes: Walk the chain step by step, pausing on step 3 as the single avoidable mistake. This maps directly to a frequent interview question on why S3 breaches recur despite provider security.

slides.title: Tools And Next Step
slides.lead: Catching a wrong assumption before it becomes an incident means checking the customer-owned settings directly, not trusting that the platform already handled them

points.text: AWS Trusted Advisor flags public buckets and open security groups
IAM Access Analyzer reviews policies for unintended external access
AWS Well-Architected security pillar lists customer-owned checks

note.text: A single tool catching one misconfiguration is not enough; durable protection needs several independent controls across network, identity, data, application and monitoring layers

slides.notes: Mention that these checks are detective, not preventive, so a layered set of controls is still needed. Tie this to the recurring exam angle: detection tools alone do not fix a responsibility gap.

slides.title: Layered Security Model
slides.lead: A single control can fail or be bypassed, so cloud security stacks several independent defenses instead of trusting one. Defense in depth spreads protection across network, identity, data, application and monitoring layers

items: Network: filters traffic at the perimeter and between subnets
Identity: verifies who or what is making each request
Data: protects information at rest and in transit
Application: hardens the code and runtime handling requests
Monitoring: detects and alerts on suspicious activity

slides.notes: Introduce defense in depth as the umbrella over all five layers about to be covered. Ask: why is one strong firewall not enough on its own? Exam hook: definition plus the five standard layers.

slides.label: Analogy: airport
slides.title: Layered Security Model
slides.notes:
TR analogy: Like an airport: a security check at the entrance, a boarding-pass check at the gate, locked cockpit doors, and CCTV across the terminal. Passing one check doesn't get anyone everywhere, just as cloud security layers independent controls so breaching one layer does not expose the whole system.

Introduce defense in depth as the umbrella over all five layers about to be covered. Ask: why is one strong firewall not enough on its own? Exam hook: definition plus the five standard layers.

slides.title: Perimeter And Access
slides.lead: Network controls stop unwanted traffic from reaching resources at all, while identity controls decide what an already-connected caller may do. Together they form the first two layers an attacker meets

items: AWS Shield absorbs and mitigates distributed denial-of-service traffic
AWS WAF, the Web Application Firewall, blocks common web exploits
Security groups and network ACLs filter traffic by port and source
Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies grant only needed actions
Multi-factor authentication adds a second proof beyond a password

slides.notes: Explain that network filters stop traffic before it is processed, while identity decides what it may then do. Point to the AWS WAF and IAM console as the real locations for these controls. Exam hook: WAF stops application-layer attacks, Shield stops volumetric floods.

slides.title: Protecting The Payload
slides.lead: Once traffic and identity are verified, the remaining risk sits inside the data itself and the application code that processes it. These two layers protect what the earlier layers let through

items: Encryption at rest: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) manages the keys
Encryption in transit: TLS protects data moving between client and server
Input validation: the application rejects malformed or malicious requests
Patch management: regular updates close known software vulnerabilities
Secure coding avoids known flaws such as injection attacks

slides.notes: Clarify that data protection covers both stored and moving data, while application controls protect the code itself. Point to the KMS console and a sample WAF rule. Exam hook: difference between encryption at rest and in transit.

slides.title: The Final Layer
slides.lead: Even with every other layer in place, something can still slip through, so continuous monitoring catches what prevention missed. This layer closes the loop by detecting and alerting on real activity

items: AWS CloudTrail records API activity in the account: who did what, and when
Amazon CloudWatch tracks metrics and triggers alarms on thresholds
Amazon GuardDuty analyses logs for threats using machine learning
Alerts feed incident response so unusual activity gets investigated fast

slides.notes: Stress that monitoring does not prevent an attack but shortens how long it goes unnoticed. Point to the CloudTrail event history and GuardDuty findings screens. Exam hook: CloudTrail logs API activity, CloudWatch handles metrics and alarms.

slides.title: Controls And Purpose
slides.lead: Each layer answers a different question (what traffic, who, what data, what code and what happened) and each service is placed in the layer where it mainly acts

cells.text: Systems Manager Patch Manager, Amazon Inspector

slides.notes: Use this table to show each layer is distinct in purpose, though a few services touch more than one layer. Point to the AWS Example column as where each service is actually used. Exam hook: expect a question asking which layer a given service belongs to.

slides.title: Bridging Forward
slides.lead: Defense in depth succeeds when a failure in one layer still leaves four others standing between an attacker and the resource. No single control is assumed to be perfect

points.text: Layers are designed to be independent: one failed layer should not disable another
Coverage must span prevention, such as network and identity, and detection
Identity-layer decisions are often the hardest to get right, and stolen credentials are a common attack path

slides.notes: Close by noting identity decisions are often the hardest layer to get right in practice, setting up the detailed access rules that follow. Exam hook: identity is frequently the layer attackers target first, via stolen credentials.

1. Security Goals: Confidentiality, integrity & availability in the cloud
2. Shared Responsibility Model: Security of the cloud vs security in the cloud
3. Responsibility by Service Model: Boundary shifts across IaaS, PaaS & SaaS
4. Common Misunderstandings: Provider vs customer duties; incidents caused by wrong assumptions
5. Defense in Depth: Layered controls: network, identity, data, application & monitoring
